transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Well, student health actually sent me here. They're refusing to clear me for these youth workshops I want to do because they say my weight is too low. I mean, I guess the number has kept dropping, but to me it just feels like... well, it's just what happens when I’m really focused and busy with my classes.
When you're eating, are you intentionally limiting how much you eat or avoiding certain foods to keep your weight down?

Yes, I guess I do intentionally limit it. I actually plan my whole day around not really eating. Like, I'll just have coffee before my studio classes, and maybe I'll take a few bites of something from the café if people are watching me, just so they don't say anything. 

But I definitely avoid certain foods on purpose. I stay away from bread, or really anything oily. It just... it feels like eating those things would completely undo all the control I’ve worked so hard for.

Do you ever have episodes where you eat a large amount of food in a short period of time and feel like you've lost control during that eating? And if so, do you do anything afterward to try to compensate, like making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising excessively?

No, I don't really do that. I don't have times where I eat a lot of food at once or feel out of control like that. My focus is just on keeping my eating very restricted and controlled. So I don't do any of those things afterward either, like throwing up or taking laxatives, because I don't really eat enough to feel like I need to undo it in that way.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with anorexia nervosa, restrictive type. She demonstrates intentional severe dietary restriction with caloric limitation, avoidance of specific food categories (bread, oily foods), preoccupation with control over eating, significantly low body weight (documented by student health as concerning enough to restrict participation), and distorted cognition regarding the consequences of eating. Absence of binge-eating or compensatory behaviors (purging, laxative use, excessive exercise) rules out binge-eating/purging type. The restriction is driven by desire for control and fear that eating would 'undo' her progress, consistent with restrictive-type anorexia nervosa.
